Imereti

Kutaisi, Gelati and a karst landscape — caves, canyons and waterfalls within an hour of each other.

Click a marker for details. Coloured lines are ready-made road trips.

Imereti is the heart of western Georgia and the region where the climate visibly changes: the air is humid, the vegetation thicker and the winter much milder than in the east. Its centre is Kutaisi, one of the oldest cities in the country and heir to the kingdom of Colchis, today a busy place of markets, the Rioni river and Bagrati Cathedral on its hill.

Ten kilometres out of town stands Gelati Monastery, founded by King David the Builder in 1106 as both a monastery and an academy, UNESCO-listed and the single most important store of Georgian mosaic and fresco painting. Small Motsameta sits nearby on a bend above the gorge, on a rock spur with a drop on three sides.

The second layer here is karst. Prometheus Cave offers long lit galleries and an underground river; Sataplia Nature Reserve combines dinosaur footprints with a cave and a glass viewing platform; Okatse Canyon is crossed by a metal walkway suspended above the gorge; Kinchkha Waterfall drops in stages down a limestone wall. North-east, near Chiatura, the Katskhi Pillar rises some forty metres with a small church on top. To the south, Sairme is a mineral water resort in the forest.

The season is long. Caves and churches work all year, while canyons and waterfalls are best from May to October, since the walkways get slippery in winter. Two days is a comfortable minimum with a night in Kutaisi, and the region fits neatly into any longer route west.

Best for

  • A two-day base in Kutaisi
  • Gelati and Bagrati in a single morning
  • Caves and canyons with children
  • A stop on the way to Batumi or Svaneti

Driving conditions

Getting into Imereti means crossing the Likhi range. The main E60 runs over the Rikoti Pass and has been rebuilt in stages with new tunnels and bridges; parts are open, and on other parts you can still meet construction detours and delays, so allow slack in the schedule rather than a precise arrival time. As far as Kutaisi and inside the city the asphalt is good and an economy car is enough.

Access roads to the sites are uneven. Gelati and Prometheus are reached on asphalt; the last stretch to Okatse is rougher; and the road to Kinchkha Waterfall is gravel that deteriorates markedly after rain, which is where ground clearance stops being optional. Morning fog is common and western Georgian rain arrives without much warning, so plan on driving slowly rather than making up time. Fuel is easy in Kutaisi, Zestaponi and Khoni, less so in the villages beyond them.
